doc.title: Jay Leonhart interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Pay in the early 1960s, Buddy Morrow, and drinking his way out of New York
summary: He earned $150 a week with Buddy Morrow and in New York, then left in 1963 because of drinking, worked in insurance in Baltimore, and returned sober in 1967.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: What was a club date paying in the early ‘60s?

Well I think — I went on the road, let me see I went on the road with Woody, no not with Woody Herman, with Buddy Morrow’s band in 1959, ‘60, for $150 a week, and saved almost all of it, came back with more money than I had ever had in my life. Then I went © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-

to New York, I think I was making $150 a week in 1961. I mean whatever that came to a night, it was six nights. And I was paying rent and my apartment was $150 a month, I had six rooms, five rooms on Riverside Drive for $150 a month, and I could have kept it. I could have kept it and today it would be $600. But I gave it up, and left New York in 1963. I had been drinking too much. You know I was a kid and I just wasn’t in shape for that kind of thing. And I was messing around and drinking and so I left, unhappy, in ‘63, and went back to Baltimore. I started to work for my father, and realized that — I started working in the insurance business with my father in his company. And I went to a sales course and I realized wait a minute, you can’t be drunk and you can’t be drugged and sell life insurance. You just — I’m not going to do it. It finally dawned on me. And I said you probably can’t play music well either in that condition. And it took me four years to really stop drinking, to really start care of myself, which I did. And in 1967 I moved back to New York. I really wanted to play. I knew I didn’t want to — and I was completely sober. And I was able to really tackle the difficulties of earning a living as a musician.
